nodes.name: m-WO3 hydrothermal synthesis and annealing
nodes.procedure: The synthesis of m-WO3 was firstly conducted using a hydrothermal method reported by Shim Joo et al. [35] with some modification. Typically, 1g of ammonium (para)tungstate hydrate was added in 25 mL deionized water (DI water) and then 3.1 mL of HCl (3 mol L-1) was drop wise into the solution with strong agitation for fully precipitating the H2WO4. After stirring for 1h, the yellow gelatinous precipitate was formed. Subsequently, 2 mL of H2O2 was added with vigorously stirred for another 1h with the transparent solution (peroxopolytungstic acid) was formed. Two pieces of W mesh (25×35 mm) which were previously washed with acetone, isopropyl alcohol (IPA), ethanol, and DI water in sequence, were leaned against the wall of a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave and the as-prepared precursor solution was filled into the reactor. The hydrothermal synthesis was carried out at 160°C for 12 h. After reaction, the as-prepared samples were rinsed with DI water, dried, and further annealed at 500°C for 2 h. The obtained electrodes were marked as m-WO3/W mesh. Moreover, the samples annealed at 400°C for 2 h were marked as h-WO3/W mesh.

nodes.name: hm-m-WO3 phase junction synthesis
nodes.procedure: In order to obtain the hexagonal-monoclinic phase junction WO3 (hm-m-WO3), a mixed phase of hexagonal and monoclinic WO3 (hm-WO3) was constructed on m-WO3 through the second-step hydrothermal treatment [36]. In detail, 0.5g of ammonium (para)tungstate hydrate was added into 30 mL DI water. And 350 μL of concentrated HCl (36% - 38%) dropped into the above solution with vigorously stirred for 0.5h. Therefore, 1mL of H2O2 and 0.25g of citric acid were added into the gel with continuous stirring for 1h to form precursor solution. Two pieces of as-prepared m-WO3 were placed at the angle against the wall of the 50 mL Teflon-lined autoclave, and the precursor solution was filled into it. Subsequently, the sealed autoclave was heated at 160°C for 12h and was allowed to cool down naturally. The obtained electrodes were washed and calcined at 475°C for 1h, which was marked hm-m-WO3.

nodes.characterization_summary: hm-m-WO3/W mesh shows mixed phases of hexagonal (JCPDS No. 75-2187) and monoclinic WO3 (JCPDS No. 71-2141); m-WO3 shows pure monoclinic phase.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of hm-m- WO₃/W mesh (Fig. 1a) shows the mixed phases that include hexagonal and monoclinic WO₃ (JCPDS No. 75-2187 and No. 71-2141).

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman 532 nm: hm-m-WO3 matches m-WO3 monoclinic peaks; 457 nm: hm-m-WO3 shows monoclinic peaks (270, 326, 714, 809 cm⁻¹) and hexagonal peaks (251, 690 cm⁻¹).
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 1b, Raman spectra excited by 532-nm laser, hm-m- WO₃ exhibits the same signals as m- WO₃ and these peaks match well with the monoclinic WO₃. However, Raman peaks of hm-m- WO₃ with a 457-nm laser (Fig. 1c) show six Raman bands, in which the peaks at around 270, 326, 714, and 809 cm⁻¹ can be assigned to the monoclinic WO₃, and peaks at 251 and 690 cm⁻¹ are corresponding to the hexagonal WO₃.

nodes.characterization_summary: hm-m-WO3/W mesh shows thick WO3 films with 3D network structure, average thickness 18.5 μm; m-WO3 shows nanoplate structure ~9 μm thick; hm-m-WO3 shows nanoplates with hexagonal prisms.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of hm-m- WO₃/W mesh photoanode show that the thick WO₃ films grown on the smoothfaced W mesh with a 3-D structure, and the average thickness of hm-m WO₃ is 18.5 μm.

nodes.characterization_summary: hm-m-WO3 interface shows clear phase boundary; monoclinic WO3: 0.365 nm (200), 0.377 nm (020); hexagonal WO3: 0.632 nm (010/100); angles 90° monoclinic, 120° hexagonal.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of hm-m- WO₃ which are taken from the interface region show a clear phase boundary between monoclinic and hexagonal WO₃... lattice spacing of 0.365 nm and 0.377 nm are corresponding to the (200) and (020) planes of the monoclinic WO₃, respectively, and the lattice spacing of 0.632 nm is consistent with the d value of the (010) and (100) planes of hexagonal WO₃.

nodes.characterization_summary: Work functions: W mesh 5.32 eV, m-WO3 4.82 eV, confirming Schottky junction formation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The work functions of metallic W mesh and m WO₃ are obtained as 5.32 eV and 4.82 eV, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: h-WO3 absorption edge 445 nm (bandgap 2.72 eV), m-WO3 425 nm (2.92 eV), hm-m-WO3 426 nm (2.87 eV).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The prepared h- WO₃, m- WO₃, and hm-m- WO₃ show optical absorption edge at ca. 445, 425, and 426 nm, respectively. The optical bandgap of these samples can be determined by the Tauc formula... and the calculated bandgaps of h- WO₃, m- WO₃ and hm-m- WO₃ are 2.72, 2.92, and 2.87 eV, respectively.

nodes.evidence_snippet: The PL intensity of hm-m- WO₃ dramatically decreases in comparison with h- WO₃ and m- WO₃, indicating the reduced amount of carrier recombination.

nodes.characterization_summary: Average lifetimes: h-WO3 5.80 ns, m-WO3 5.96 ns, hm-m-WO3 6.21 ns; longest lifetime for hm-m-WO3 due to heterophase junction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The average lifetime of h- WO₃, m- WO₃, and hm-m- WO₃ is calculated to be 5.80, 5.96, and 6.21 ns, respectively (Table S1).

nodes.characterization_summary: hm-m-WO3/W mesh shows smallest arc radius under light illumination, indicating fastest charge transfer kinetics.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The hm-m- WO₃/W mesh with light illumination exhibits the smallest arc radius of the EIS plots among the WO₃ electrode, which suggests the fastest charge transfer kinetics.
